flags.issue: Answer-position leak: in the source file the correct option is A for every one of the 140 mc items, and every ms item's correct set is the leading options (A,B or A,B,C) with only the final option wrong. Unless options are shuffled at render time, every item is answerable by position alone. A second cue: wrong options are often padded with long qualifying clauses (e.g. b2-09 B, b3-01 C, b4-06 C, b5-01 D, c1-method-m2 B), so the shortest plain option is usually the key.

Factual error: mica's T-O-T sheets are held together by interlayer K+ cations, which are relatively weak ionic bonds. They are not held by 'weak intermolecular forces' (van der Waals); that describes graphite, talc and pyrophyllite. The keyed answer A is therefore incorrect as worded, and distractor D ('ionic bonds that dissolve in air') mixes the actual bond type with nonsense.

Fracture zone is defined as a 'linear step in the seafloor offsetting a ridge'. The feature that actually offsets the ridge is the active transform fault. A fracture zone is the inactive scar beyond the ridge segments. This contradicts c3-transform-m1 and c3-transform-p1 in the same bank.

The stem says ridge offsets are 'connected by fracture zones'. They are connected by transform faults; fracture zones are the inactive extensions (compare c3-transform-m1). The key A ('Only on the segment between the offset ridge crests') is also overstated, because the ridge crests themselves have shallow earthquakes. C ('Only at the ridge crests') is partly true too, so neither 'only' statement is fully correct.

The stem gives no thicknesses and the diagram spec ({showDensity:true}) specifies none, but the keyed reasoning depends on A being 'the thickest'. As written, a sufficiently thick denser block C could still stand higher, so the item cannot be answered from the stem. The needed fact appears only inside option A.

The order of 'shallow sea deposits a gray layer' versus 'sand dunes deposit a sand layer' cannot be determined from the text. Both stackings are geologically common (e.g. Coconino dune sandstone overlain by marine Toroweap/Kaibab). The answer depends entirely on an unseen slide, which is not shown as a diagram.

Seven-step order with more than one defensible sequence. 'Make a model of interpretation' can reasonably come before testing (the model generates predictions) or at the end. 'Observe' and 'Describe' are often simultaneous. The item needs the lecture's exact list and has no diagram or reference.

This is a course-specific procedure that cannot be derived from geology knowledge. 'Predict' before 'Research' and 'Research' before 'Predict' are both defensible, and 'Draw' versus 'Justify' order is arbitrary without the lecture slide.

Stating that lava domes are built 'in one episode' conflicts with b5-12 in this same bank. Mount St. Helens' dome grew through many extrusive episodes in 1980-86 and again in 2004-08. Many domes are polygenetic over years, so the 'one episode' classification is at best a simplification.

A concordant basalt sheet between two sandstone layers with vertical columns fits a buried lava flow just as well as a sill. Distinguishing them requires a baked upper contact, inclusions of the upper layer, or a weathered/vesicular top. The key works only because option D's reason ('sills do not have joints') is false, not because the observations rule out a lava flow.

Ambiguous wording: 'crystallize in the same order in which they melt' can be read by temperature sequence (olivine highest-T for both crystallizing and melting — i.e., the 'same' temperature ordering) or by time sequence on cooling vs heating (reverse order). Intended answer is presumably False (reverse order), but a student reasoning by temperature could defend True. Reword, e.g., 'The first mineral to crystallize on cooling is also the first to melt on heating.'

'Dominant in mafic and ultramafic rocks' is ambiguous: Ca-rich plagioclase (C) is dominant in mafic rocks (gabbro/basalt) but not in ultramafic rocks (peridotite). If 'and' means both, C is wrong; if it means either, C is right. Specify 'mafic or ultramafic' or split the question.

More than one defensible order: many versions of the scientific-method template (including textbook sequences) begin with Question before Observation, or with Observation before Question. The key's placement of these first two steps must match the specific Lecture 2 slide; otherwise both orders are defensible.

Distractor B (heat left over from Earth's formation) is arguably also correct: current geophysical estimates (e.g., geoneutrino data) put radiogenic heat at roughly half of Earth's surface heat flow, with primordial heat supplying much of the rest. Also 'mostly in the mantle' is debatable since heat-producing elements are most concentrated in continental crust. Keep only if the textbook states radioactive decay supplies most heat.

Option D (clam shell of CaCO3) is contested: under the strict 'inorganic' textbook definition it is excluded, but the IMA and many modern textbooks accept biogenic calcite/aragonite as minerals. Students aware of that could select D. Consider replacing with an unambiguous non-mineral (e.g., coal, amber).
